resources.string: Calculate physical length, electrical length and phase delay using the cable velocity factor.
VF is entered manually. The initial value 0.66 is an example, not a specification for your cable. Use the manufacturer’s data or a measurement.
Cable velocity factor and antenna shortening factor describe different physical quantities. Set them independently.
Phase changes by 360° over one wavelength in the cable. A quarter wavelength gives 90° and a half wavelength gives 180°. The horizontal axis shows positive phase lag along the line.

At 145 MHz and VF = 0.66, the electrical length is 7.3283 wavelengths or 2638.189°. The scale spans eight periods. Seven complete periods and the remainder of 118.189° are filled. With the usual phase convention, the transmission phase of a matched line in this example is −118.189° modulo 360°.

The model describes a uniform cable between reference planes A and B and uses VF at the selected frequency. The delay covers a single pass from A to B without reflections.

The model omits connector effects, line discontinuities, loss and frequency dispersion. A constant VF is suitable for estimates over a band where it varies little. Check load matching separately.

For precise cable assembly trimming, verify the electrical length by measurement, for example with a vector network analyzer (VNA).

Electrical length describes the phase lag a wave accumulates as it travels through the cable at a given frequency. The velocity factor VF is the ratio of the phase velocity in the cable to the speed of light in vacuum.

At the same frequency, a lower VF gives a shorter wavelength in the cable. A shorter physical section therefore gives the same electrical length.

Electrical length can be expressed in degrees, radians, fractions of a wavelength or equivalent meters in vacuum. In wavelengths it is φ/360° = L/λc, where φ is the phase lag in degrees, L is the physical length, and λc = VF·c/f is the wavelength in the cable. The equivalent length L/VF gives the same phase lag in vacuum at frequency f.

The value modulo 360° is the remainder of the calculated lag after removing complete turns. For example, 450° leaves 90°. When comparing with measured S₂₁ transmission phase, account for its sign and reference planes.

Phase delay is the time equivalent of the phase lag of a sinusoid at the selected frequency. It equals φ/(360°·f) = L/(VF·c). Group delay describes the delay of a narrowband envelope and follows from the slope of the unwrapped transmission phase versus frequency. Both delays coincide in the constant-VF model. With significant dispersion, group delay can differ. Estimating it requires transmission phase as a function of frequency, for example an S₂₁ measurement across the band.
A cable between reference planes A and B. Phase delay refers to one pass from A to B, without reflections or connectors.
Enter a complete nonnegative decimal number, up to 32 characters. Signs and scientific notation are not supported.
Complete the selected inputs to see the result.
Phase velocity equals cable velocity factor times the speed of light in vacuum.
Electrical length in degrees equals 360 times frequency times physical length divided by phase velocity. Phase delay from A to B equals physical length divided by phase velocity.
Physical length equals electrical length in degrees times phase velocity, divided by the product of 360 and frequency.
